messages.body_plain:
The Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling (CREEM) is hosting two linked workshops in the summer of 2016 at the University of St. Andrews, Scotland. This second announcement is to note

·         Workshop registration is now open (see website URL at bottom of this note to reserve a place)

·         As part of the registration fee, participants will receive the 2015 book Distance Sampling: Methods and Application by Buckland et al. that focuses upon topics of relevance to distance sampling practitioners.  The case studies found in this book will form the basis of both the introductory and advanced workshops.

The first workshop (16-19 August) will run at an introductory level, and will focus on distance sampling methods, largely described in the standard reference book "Introduction to Distance Sampling." The workshop will be a blend of theory and practice and participants will learn how to use the program "Distance." Participants will gain a solid grounding in both survey design and methods of analysis for distance sampling surveys.

The advanced distance sampling workshop (22-25 August) will include advanced treatment of analyses in which detectability on the transect line is not assumed to be perfect (the so-called g(0) problem) and spatial (or density surface) modelling. We will showcase a series of R packages for performing standard as well as sophisticated analyses in R.

For all workshops, participants are encouraged to bring their own data sets, and can expect to perform preliminary analyses of their data.  Participants can use our computers or bring their own laptops.

Additional details regarding the workshop contents and registration details can be found at our website

http://creem2.st-andrews.ac.uk/distance-sampling-workshops-st-andrews-august-2016-2/

messages.subject: Expected cluster size
messages.body_plain:
Dear Distance Samplers

When working with clustered data, DISTANCE software can be used to estimate expected cluster size via a regression approach. Page 75 of Intro to Distance Sampling (Reprint 2011) describes an approach to investigate size bias, namely the regression of cluster size (or log cluster size) on distance is expected to have a POSITIVE slope, while a regression of cluster size (or log cluster size) on probability of detection g(i) to have a NEGATIVE slope.

Page 121 of the same text shows Fig 4.3 which is a graphic of the former combination above. Does anyone know of a reference which has graphics of the latter combination - log cluster size versus detection probability please?

I am reading a paper at the moment that interprets a NEGATIVE slope of log(s(i)) on g(x(i)) as being somewhat detrimental, "... lead to a regression line with a negative slope, and thus the computed expected group size was lower than the observed group size. Using these results is likely to lead to increased inaccuracy". Does this seem sound judgement?

Also, when characterizing a detection function, we need some data. I guess the more bins to the Perpendicular Distance axis the better - 3 or less too few, 5 or more desirable? Then, as a guide, how many clusters (or individuals) are needed to accurately define a detection function? Maybe 200, 300 ...? Some managers desire an estimate of animal population within quite a small specific area, where only 20 or 30 clusters have been spotted. I worry that this is too few to use to estimate a detection function.

Any thoughts or experiences would be appreciated.

Regards, Terry

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Expected cluster size
messages.body_plain:
Terry

You've done a lot of detective work to try to sort out the matter of size bias regression.  I had a look through some reprints in search of a graph of ln(cluster size) vs g-hat(x) and I failed to find a figure.  However, here is a figure we use as part of our distance sampling training materials, showing 4 combinations of independent and response variable transformed and untransformed, with the combination about which you are asking highlighted:

In each instance the horizontal arrow is pointing at the size-bias adjusted estimate of expected group size.  As you suggest, the slope of the relationship of ln(cluster size) vs g-hat(x) is negative.  The adjusted estimate of group size should be smaller than the mean size of observed clusters, because the detection process tends to miss the small clusters at large perpendicular distances.  g-hat(x) is closer to 1 at small distances from the transect, which is why the slope is reversed when g-hat(x) is used as the independent variable as opposed to x as the dependent variable.  Hence you are justified in questioning what you have read .

Think of bins as "points of support" for detection function modelling.  Those points of support serve two purposes: a) characterising the shape of the detection function and b) assessing the goodness of fit of detection function to data (when using chi-square GOF testing, which is all that is available when data are binned at time of collection).  When fitting a 2-parameter hazard rate model to 3 bin data, there are no degrees of freedom remaining after fitting to assess goodness of fit.  That can serve as a guide about number of bins during analysis; however, data collection in the field may place additional constraints upon reliable placement of detections into the proper bin.

The question "how many detections are needed to characterise a detection function" comes up often.  For line transects, we recommend 60-80 detections (see Buckland et al. 2015:23  Distance sampling: methods and applications), however if the data are "well behaved" then reasonable results can arise from fewer detections.  If there are multiple strata (either geographic or treating species as strata), some gains can arise from using strata as a covariate in the detection function modelling.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Terry,

Just to add to what Eric said, regarding your first question about the authors of a paper you were reading and cluster size bias regression. Indeed one would expect in most circumstances that the observed mean cluster size might be higher than the true mean cluster size, since larger groups are easier to detect (but note a possible opposite effect could be observed if say you tended to underestimate group sizes away from the line only!).

Since you provided a verbatim sentence I used google to track it down, there's only 1 hit, so this must be the paper you were reading:

http://crowhops.com/category/uncategorized/page/198/

When one looks in there the authors seem to believe that group sizes are underestimated from the air, based on a previous survey. This is the reason they then state that the size bias regression is leading to problems, because they already believe that the group sizes they have estimated are underestimating the true group sizes, so they do not want an analysis that makes the mean group size even smaller. Not sure this is is a sound strategy. Without seeing the data is hard to make additional comments, but I note that there are at least two problems involved (1. size bias; 2. underestimation of group size) and the way these interact will dictate how one should move forward. But in my opinion, it is not sound to state that you should ignore the size bias, you are trying to trade biases with different directions but unknown magnitudes.

hope this helps

Tiago

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Eric and Tiago for your prompt replies.

Eric, thanks very much for the graphic of expected group size. After I sent my questions yesterday, I was working my way through your very informative videos at http://distancesampling.org/videos.html and at about 16:35 minutes into the Distance Sampling Assumptions II video, heard you make mention of a Clustered Populations lecture. I don't think this is available yet to folk outside your Training Courses.

Also, I found your Assumptions II video to offer the suggestion to aim for >60 data points upon which to form a frequency histogram and thence the detection function. The Detection Function video also reminded me that the model complexity - the numbers of parameters to estimate in the detection function and any added series expansion - will be limited should the number of distance bins be restrictingly small.

Tiago, thanks for reminding me that situations could arise where the slope of this regression could be significantly positive, as outlined also on page 75 of the Intro to Distance Sampling text. Such is a dilemma when analysing clustered data; which estimate of group size do you use - the mean observed group size from the air survey (and assume accuracy), a size-bias corrected estimate of group size from the same survey, an estimate from an earlier aerial survey of the same area, an estimate from a ground survey conducted some years earlier, or something else.

Thanks for sharing your knowledge, Terry

Glad you found the videos Terry.  You are correct that I've not made the clusters lecture material available on line.

One comment on your final thought regarding what estimate of group size to use.  Presented with the choices you pose, I would use data collected at the same time from the same platform as data that will be used to estimate group density.  That way I need not make assumptions about constancy of group size over time or constant with sighting conditions.  Similar discussions take place when needing to estimate g(0) because not all animals are seen on the transect; what estimate of g(0) do you use?  An estimate coming from the data collected on the same survey, or an estimate from another place or time?

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Warning: Size bias adjustment has increased expected cluster size.
messages.body_plain:
Iakha

Distance has provided you with a warning, suggesting that something unexpected occurred when analysing your data.  I suggest you look at section 3.5 of Buckland et al. (2001) that discusses analysis of data for animals that occur in clusters.

An important element of analysing such data is the estimation of average cluster size.  This is made difficult because large clusters are more likely to be seen at large distances than small clusters; hence the average of detected clusters is likely larger than the average size of clusters in the population.  This is termed the "size bias" problem.  By default, Distance performs a regression in an attempt to remove this size bias, and produce an adjusted estimate of "expected cluster size".

The expectation is that this adjusted estimate will be smaller that the observed average cluster size.  The warning message in your case states this is not the case, an instead the adjusted estimate is larger that the observed average cluster size.  There are several reasons that may cause this.  Often, this arises because of small numbers of clusters either in the study or in strata within the study area.  I suggest you examine the number of observations in your data and the observed cluster sizes.  It may be the case there is no size bias in your data and you were able to see clusters of all sizes equally well at all distances.  If you believe this to be the case, you can select the option in Distance on the Cluster Size tab of the Model Definition Properties to "Use mean of observed clusters"  (see below)

messages.body_plain:
Àngel

Welcome to the Distance sampling list.  I hope you are learning from reading the questions and answers of others.

Recognise that including covariates in your detection function help to explain variation in detectability, rather than variation in abundance.

If your interest is in abundance estimation by habitat and elevation, then you will want to produce multiple abundance estimates (for various combinations of habitat and elevation).  In this case, I would have thought you would have subdivided your study area into, say, elevation bands (0-500m, 500-1000m, 1000-1500m, or whatever elevations are biologically relevant) and perhaps also habitat types within elevation band.  You could then place survey effort into those habitat:elevation strata and proceed to model detectability and produce abundance estimates.

You will struggle to produce elevation-specific abundance estimates if you treat elevation as a continuous variable.

I realise this does not address the warning messages you receive when performing your MCDS analysis, but I suggest trying to address the large questions first, then move down to the more detailed questions.  You can produce quite sensible abundance estimates without using covariates in your detection functions.  Covariates can be helpful, but not necessary.  Is this of use to you?

Àngel

I am concentrating upon the purpose of your study.  In your first email you said the purpose was to estimate abundance of ungulates by habitat and elevation.  Did you then allocate survey effort in such a manner that you can produce estimates for the areas of interest to you?

Reading your messages, it sounds as if you did not have habitat and elevation in your mind at the time you designed where your transects were placed.

Estimation at the sample level is awkward because this does not permit inference beyond the transects you surveyed.  I presume you are hoping to make inference to all of the area with habitat of type "A".  In that case, you would need replicate transects in habitat type "A" and variability between replicate transects will tell you something about how variable abundance is within that habitat type.

What I would suggest instead, is as you say, assigning each transect to a 'dominant' habitat (and elevation?) type.  You might then use "Post-stratification" by habitat/elevation type.  The challenge here will be whether these habitat/elevation combination will occur in sufficient numbers for there to be adequate effort in them to make the inferences you wish.

This is why it would have been preferable to lay out your effort incorporating your study objectives, rather than hoping in retrospect the design matches your objectives.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Few more DSM queries
messages.body_plain:
Hi Peter, hi listfolk,

First off, very glad to hear that the materials are useful!

To your questions:

1. Duchon splines: do you mean that there are still "extreme"
predictions far from the data or that the estimated abundance over the
whole study area is still too high? The former should be what Duchon
splines guard against, but as we are still experimenting with them in
practice, it's possible there are still some behaviours we're not aware
of yet. In the latter case, this is still possible as we don't guarantee
that the remaining effects in the model are zero outside the data, just
that they are constant (and that constant could be big). If it is the
former case please do contact me offlist with an example, as I'd be very
interested in taking a look. Another possible basis that you may want to
try (if you haven't already) is "ts" (thin plate splines with shrinkage)
which may be useful.

2. Temporal trends: if you have sufficient coverage, it may be possible
to build a term like: te(x, y, time, d=c(2, 1), bs=c("ts", "cr")) or
somesuch which would give you a 2d spatial term interacting with time.
That being said there are some important caveats about using this kind
of model. Specifically ensuring that the coverage of your survey is
similar year-on-year seems sensible (you don't want to predict for 2010
using data from 2006 if there was some change in distribution between
those dates and you won't know if there was if there was no survey
effort). As with Duchon splines I think this lives in the "experimental"
side of things at the moment, so it's worth being cautious.

3. More on point counts soon. This is on my todo list at the moment.

Hope this helps!

best,
--dave

messages.body_plain:
Emma

Welcome to the list.

I'm not certain about the answer to your first question about 'usable' records.  However, the value 500 is used as a cutoff associated with visualisation of the goodness of fit of the detection function to your data, when a quantile-quantile (QQ) plot is displayed.  I suspect this is the message you were seeing.  This message is benign for two reasons a) the goodness of fit tests are unaffected, only the graphical depiction is affected, and b) it is merely a warning, and the number of points displayed in the QQ plot can be changed in Model Definition Properties | Detection function tab | Diagnostics button.

Your second question I think is a misinterpretation of the sampling design that underlies distance sampling (and many other types of sampling).  It is not advisable to produce density estimates at the level of the sample (meaning transect in this context).  Presumably, you have placed replicate transects randomly through your study area.  You wish to estimate density/abundance in your study area rather than for each transect.

The warning messages Distance produces are related to your request for transect-specific detection functions and density estimates.  Messages say you have only 1 observation on a transect which is less than the number of parameters you are trying to estimate, so Distance cannot comply with your request.  Similarly, Distance notes that variability in encounter rates between transects cannot be measured when encounter rate is measured at the transect level (cannot compute a variance from a sample of size 1).

I don't know anything about your study design, but the 'usual' procedure for estimating density/abundance in a study is to request density/encounter/detection at the level of the study area; or if you conducted a stratified survey design, then you might request these quantities be estimated at the stratum level, but not at the sample level.

See if altering your analysis in that way produces far fewer warnings.
